records.sourceFile: The implementation of velocity-based training paradigm for team sports - Framework, technologies, practical recommendations and challenges.pdf

paper.citation: Balsalobre-Fernández C, Torres-Ronda L. The Implementation of Velocity-Based Training Paradigm for Team Sports: Framework, Technologies, Practical Recommendations and Challenges. Sports. 2021;9:47.
paper.abstract: A review of velocity-based training (VBT) for resistance training in team sports. It covers the limits of 1RM-based prescription, velocity-tracking technologies, individual load-velocity profiling, combining velocity with repetitions in reserve, velocity-loss thresholds, and monitoring of individual performance trends. The authors present practical recommendations and discuss the limits of 'muscle power' measurement from velocity devices.
paper.tldr: Velocity-based training uses bar speed to set and check loads, so training can match each athlete's daily capacity. For team sports, the authors recommend individual load-velocity profiles, consistent validated devices, and repetitions in reserve for exercises without velocity tracking.
paper.methods: Narrative review and practical framework. The paper describes no search strategy. It uses worked examples, a load-velocity profiling protocol with 4 to 6 incremental loads, and an illustrative 8-week load table, with no new data collected.
paper.findings: The authors argue that 1RM-based loads can be inaccurate on a given day, and that load-velocity relationships differ by exercise, athlete and training status. Velocity-tracking devices differ in validity and reliability, and 'power' calculated from velocity alone can misrepresent the true output. Velocity loss of about 10 to 20 percent is cited as giving similar physical gains to larger losses with less volume, and a profile R2 below 0.92 is suggested as a prompt to repeat the test.
paper.limitations: The paper does not describe how sources were selected or appraised, and it presents no new data. Recommendations are largely expert-based and the examples are individual cases; the velocity-loss thresholds come from cited studies, while the R2 cut-off of 0.92 is stated as the authors' experience. Injury prevention is named as an aim without supporting evidence in the text.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches of large team-sport squads can measure bar velocity in a warm-up set and adjust loads that day, rebuild load-velocity profiles every 4 to 6 weeks, and use repetitions in reserve for exercises without velocity measurement. Device choice should stay consistent, and 'muscle power' from a velocity device should not be treated as a measure of true power.
paper.athleteDev: Developing team-sport athletes can be trained with individual load-velocity profiles and velocity thresholds that track their progress. The paper suggests that load-velocity profiles change with training, so profiles should be rechecked as athletes develop.
paper.rtp: The paper mentions return to play only in passing in its introduction and offers no return-to-play protocol or evidence. It cannot be used to decide when an injured athlete is ready to load or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: The maximal intensity period - Rationalizing its use in team sports practice.pdf

paper.citation: Weaving D, Young D, Riboli A, Jones B, Coratella G. The Maximal Intensity Period: Rationalising its Use in Team Sports Practice. Sports Medicine - Open. 2022;8:128.
paper.abstract: This conceptual review describes how the maximal intensity period (MIP) is determined in team sports, compares it with whole-match averages, and sets out when MIP can and cannot guide training. The authors conclude that MIP is far above match averages and does not capture internal load.
paper.tldr: Match MIP values are much higher than averages, so they may help evaluate the intensity of some technical-tactical drills such as small-sided games, although the authors call this use inconclusive. They should not be used to set intensity for interval, repeated sprint or linear speed training.
paper.methods: Conceptual review with no described search strategy. The authors summarise MIP calculation methods (fixed epochs, moving averages and a power-law model) and compare MIP with whole-match means using data from earlier studies.
paper.findings: MIP for total distance was about 160 to 251 percent greater than whole-match means in rugby union, rugby league, Australian football and Gaelic football. In elite soccer, about 61 percent of total distance was covered above the match mean. Small-sided games in Ligue 1 and Premier League soccer and in rugby league generally sat below match MIP values for average and high-speed running, although mechanical load was likely higher in 4v4 games than in matches.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and its study selection is not systematic. The comparisons rely on different devices, speed thresholds and populations. MIP does not account for internal load, and the authors state it is inconclusive whether MIP can evaluate technical-tactical training, calling for intervention studies on MIP-based training.
paper.practicalImplications: Compare a drill's average and high-speed distance per minute with the match MIP for the same duration to judge whether technical-tactical drills such as small-sided games are under- or over-loading players, bearing in mind the authors call this use unproven. Do not use match MIP to prescribe interval, repeated sprint or linear speed work; use individual measures such as maximal aerobic speed or critical speed instead.
paper.athleteDev: Use match MIP for the exact duration of a drill to check whether small-sided games reach the match peak demands for high-speed running. Do not use it as the target speed for conditioning intervals or sprint work.
paper.rtp: This review does not address return to sport and cannot be used to set rehabilitation running intensities. The authors state that MIP does not reflect maximal aerobic capacity or maximal speed, so it should not replace those measures in rehab running.

records.sourceFile: The muscle morphology of elite sprint running.pdf

paper.citation: Miller R, Balshaw TG, Massey GJ, Maeo S, Lanza MB, Johnston M, et al. The Muscle Morphology of Elite Sprint Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020.
paper.abstract: Muscle volumes (MRI) and isometric strength were compared in elite sprinters, sub-elite sprinters and untrained controls, and related to 100 m performance. Total lower-body muscle volume differed across all three groups, hip extensor and gluteus maximus volumes distinguished elite from sub-elite sprinters and tracked sprint times, and isometric strength did not separate the sprint groups.
paper.tldr: Elite sprinters had larger hip extensor and gluteus maximus volumes than sub-elite sprinters, and these muscles tracked 100 m times. With only five elite athletes and a cross-sectional design, the finding is an association and does not show that building these muscles causes faster sprinting.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 5 elite sprinters, 26 sub-elite sprinters and 11 untrained controls. Muscle volumes were measured from 3T MRI for 23 lower-limb muscles and 5 functional groups, and isometric strength was measured with dynamometers for 5 muscle groups. Groups were compared by one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests. Within the sprint cohort, Pearson correlations (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and stepwise regression related volume and strength to 100 m season's best equivalent.
paper.findings: Total lower-body volume was controls below sub-elite (+20 percent) below elite (+48 percent). Elite sprinters had greater absolute volume than sub-elite sprinters in four functional groups, with the largest difference in hip extensors (+32 percent absolute, +15 percent relative); plantarflexors did not differ between sprint groups. Gluteus maximus (+45 percent), TFL (+57 percent) and sartorius (+47 percent) were larger in elite sprinters. Across all sprinters, total volume correlated with 100 m time (r = -0.629), and absolute hip extensor volume explained 47.5 percent of the variance. Isometric strength of several groups was greater than controls in both sprint groups, but it did not differ between sprint groups and no strength measure was related to faster sprint times (relative knee extensor strength was related to slower times, r = 0.485).
paper.limitations: Only five elite sprinters were included, and the authors acknowledge the small elite sample for strength. Seven of 26 sub-elite 100 m times were estimated from 60 m or 200 m results. Strength was tested once without familiarisation, and isometric tests may lack specificity to sprinting. The cross-sectional design cannot show cause, although the authors argue a large causal component is likely.
paper.practicalImplications: In this sample, hip extensor and gluteus maximus size tracked sprint times, so coaches may track these muscle groups as part of lower-body planning for sprinters. The study does not show that increasing them causes faster sprinting, and isometric strength did not separate the two sprint groups, so it should not be the only marker of elite potential.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest that developing the hip extensors and knee flexors, for example through resistance training, would be valuable for sprinters, and the gluteus maximus findings point to targeted hypertrophy. The evidence is associative and comes from a small sample, so review progress against sprint times rather than assuming a direct effect.
paper.rtp: The study compares healthy, uninjured men and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It should not be used to set rehabilitation loads or muscle-size targets.

records.sourceFile: The perceptions and applications of cluster sets in strength and conditioning.pdf

paper.citation: Nagatani T, Vial S, Kendall KL, Comfort P, Yang J, Haff GG. The perceptions and applications of cluster sets in strength and conditioning. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2025.
paper.abstract: Forty-six strength and conditioning professionals completed an online survey on their perceptions of cluster sets and how they programme them. The authors report general alignment with published recommendations, except that cluster sets were most often used with bench press and squat variants, which require un-racking and re-racking the bar and may be physically demanding.
paper.tldr: Most coaches surveyed use cluster sets, mainly in strength-power phases, and they report raising intensity by about 2 to 15 percent of 1RM for cluster sets. Logistics such as supervising large groups and added training time are the main barriers.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey of 46 strength and conditioning professionals, recruited by email, social media and chain sampling. Closed-ended questions were analysed by frequency counts, and open-ended responses were analysed by six-stage thematic analysis.
paper.findings: 37 of 46 respondents (80 percent) used cluster sets. Strength-power phase use was reported by 31 of 37 users (84 percent), compared with 13 (35 percent) for hypertrophy or strength-endurance. Percentage of 1RM was the most common load method (23 of 37, 62 percent). Bench press and squat variants were the most common exercises. Nineteen of 37 users (51 percent) reported no concerns; the most common concerns were extended training duration (27 percent) and supervision of large groups (24 percent).
paper.limitations: Perceptions and self-reported practice only, with no athlete data. Small, self-selected sample recruited through chain sampling. The authors note that the questionnaire did not capture whether the programmes used were evidence based or the athletes' training histories.
paper.practicalImplications: Cluster sets are most often used in strength-power blocks with intensity raised by about 2 to 15 percent of 1RM, so programmes that use them should plan the added rest and supervision needed for the session. The survey cannot show whether those choices improve performance, so test them on your own athletes before relying on them.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches can use these survey patterns to plan cluster sets in strength-power phases with a load increase and longer rest, and to check that the session time and supervision are realistic for the group. The paper does not show performance gains from these choices.
paper.rtp: The study does not address rehabilitation or return to sport and should not be used to set return-to-sport loads.

records.sourceFile: The placebo and nocebo effect on sports performance - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Hurst P, Schipof-Godart L, Szabo A, Raglin J, Hettinga F, Roelands B, et al. The Placebo and Nocebo effect on sports performance: A systematic review. European Journal of Sport Science. 2020;20(3):279-292.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of placebo and nocebo effects on sport performance across 32 studies (1,513 participants) with a control or baseline condition. Small to moderate effects were found for placebo and nocebo conditions, for both nutritional and mechanical ergogenic aids. Preconditioning procedures and banned-substance placebos produced the largest effects.
paper.tldr: Placebo and nocebo effects can change sport performance by a small to moderate amount, roughly d = 0.37 on average. The evidence is low quality and highly variable, so it shows that belief matters, not how much any single aid helps.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review. Six databases were searched to March 2019 for studies of apparently healthy people or athletes that used a placebo or nocebo ergogenic aid, had a no-treatment or baseline control and reported at least one objective performance measure. Thirty-two studies were analysed using Cohen's d, with moderator analyses by aid type, placebo type and mechanism.
paper.findings: Placebo effect d = 0.36 and nocebo effect d = 0.37. Nutritional aids gave d = 0.35 and mechanical aids d = 0.47. Preconditioning procedures gave larger effects (d = 0.82) than positive (d = 0.36) or negative (d = 0.37) expectation. Overt placebos showed no average effect (d = 0.08). Anabolic steroid placebos (d = 1.44) and TENS (d = 0.86) gave large effects but from few studies.
paper.limitations: Only 4 of 32 studies had low risk of bias, and 41% did not verify that the manipulation worked. Five included studies were by the review authors, and one study's standard deviations were estimated from standard errors read off a figure. Effect sizes varied widely (pooled d = 0.37 ± 0.42), and the Abstract pooled d (0.38) differs from the Results (0.37); the Results value is reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors advise against support staff deliberately giving athletes placebos as performance aids. They suggest that building a positive, honest belief in a legitimate treatment may help it work better. Trials of performance aids should use credible placebos and measure participants' beliefs.
paper.athleteDev: Athletes may benefit more from a legitimate aid when they believe in it, so staff can build accurate, positive expectations about evidence-based strategies. This review does not support giving placebos as performance aids.
paper.rtp: This review covers acute performance tests in healthy people and athletes. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: The role of lower-limb muscle volumes in vertical jump performance in NCAA Division 1 athletes.pdf

paper.citation: O'Brien D, Ito N, Kliethermes S, Heiderscheit B. The role of lower-limb muscle volumes in vertical jump performance in NCAA Division 1 athletes. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026 (publish ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Purpose: to determine which combination of lower-extremity muscle volumes is most strongly associated with countermovement jump (CMJ) performance in 207 NCAA Division I athletes. Methods: bilateral MRI with machine-learning auto-segmentation, and CMJ height and peak power on dual force plates, with backward-selection regression adjusted for sex and sport. Results: vastus lateralis volume was related to both jump height and peak power; rectus femoris was retained for jump height, and soleus, gluteus medius, adductor magnus and biceps femoris long head for peak power. Hockey and football athletes jumped higher than basketball players, football athletes produced more peak power, and males outperformed females. Conclusions: the quadriceps, particularly the vastus lateralis, is central to CMJ performance in high-level athletes.
paper.tldr: In 207 NCAA Division I athletes, larger vastus lateralis volume was the strongest muscle correlate of both jump height and peak power. The result is a cross-sectional association in healthy athletes, so it suggests quadriceps development may matter for jumping but does not prove a training effect.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 207 NCAA Division I football, basketball, ice hockey and soccer athletes (164 male, 43 female) from one institution, cleared for full sport participation. Athletes completed bilateral CMJ testing on dual force plates and bilateral lower-limb MRI within four months of each other. Muscles were segmented automatically (38 per limb), and the 23 hip, knee and ankle flexors and extensors were normalised to body mass and height and summed across sides. Multiple regression with backward selection by BIC, with sex and sport forced in, was used for jump height and peak power, followed by a post hoc interaction test.
paper.findings: Vastus lateralis volume was associated with jump height (1.39 cm per unit of normalised volume, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.87; beta 0.36, p < .01) and peak power (1.67 W/kg, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.14; beta 0.41, p < .01). The jump height model explained R2 = 0.56 and the peak power model R2 = 0.72. Rectus femoris (p = .07) and gluteus medius (p = .06) were retained but did not reach p < .05; soleus and adductor magnus did, and biceps femoris long head was negatively associated with peak power (p = .03). Hockey (+6.63 cm) and football (+3.76 cm) athletes jumped higher than basketball players, and males jumped 8.86 cm higher and produced 8.79 W/kg more peak power than females.
paper.limitations: Single-institution, collegiate-only sample from which generalisation to recreational, high-school or professional athletes is uncertain. The cross-sectional design gives no direct evidence that hypertrophy training improves jumping, backward selection plus a post hoc test raise the risk of type I error, and muscle volume is not a measure of strength. The abstract says hockey athletes also produced more peak power than basketball players, but the results show only football differed (hockey p = .69); one author advises and one consults for the segmentation company, and the work was part-funded by the NFL.
paper.practicalImplications: Quadriceps, and vastus lateralis in particular, is the muscle group most consistently linked to jump height and peak power in this sample, so it is a reasonable focus when setting jump-performance goals for these sports. The study cannot show that adding quadriceps volume will raise jumping, so track jump outcomes alongside any hypertrophy block.
paper.athleteDev: Use CMJ height and peak power as the performance outcomes when building quadriceps-focused strength or conditioning, and expect sport and sex differences in baseline values. Benchmarks here are for healthy NCAA Division I athletes and are not targets for every squad.
paper.rtp: The sample was healthy athletes cleared for full participation, so the study does not inform return-to-sport decisions or thresholds. Its reference values may give context for healthy comparison, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: The training of short distance sprint performance in football code athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Nicholson B, Dinsdale A, Jones B, Till K. The Training of Short Distance Sprint Performance in Football Code Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of short-sprint training studies (0-20 m) in football code athletes, with moderator analyses. The review included 121 studies and 3419 athletes. Combined, secondary and tertiary training improved short-sprint performance, combined-specific training did so for 0-5 and 0-10 m, while primary and sport-only training did not. Football code, age and phase of season moderated the effects.
paper.tldr: Across 121 studies of football code athletes, combined training, resisted or assisted sprinting, and strength, power and plyometric work were each followed by faster short-sprint times. Sprinting or sport practice alone did not show a significant pre-to-post gain, and no single method was clearly best.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review, registered on OSF, searching PubMed, Cochrane, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL to 14 October 2019. Eligible studies were controlled or uncontrolled training interventions in healthy football code athletes with pre-post sprint outcomes at 20 m or less. Interventions were classified as sport-only, primary, secondary, tertiary, combined or combined-specific. Study quality was rated with the McMaster scale. Random-effects meta-analysis used standardised mean differences, with moderators for football code, sex, age, playing standard and phase of season.
paper.findings: Pooled pre-to-post SMDs for combined training were 0.92 (0-5 m), 0.60 (0-10 m) and 0.56 (0-20 m); for tertiary training 0.64, 0.56 and 0.40; and for secondary training 0.75, 0.52 and 0.64 from only 3 to 5 training groups. Combined-specific training improved 0-5 m (one group) and 0-10 m (two groups) but not 0-20 m, and primary and sport-only training showed no significant change. Combined and tertiary training produced significantly larger effects than sport-only training at all distances. Football code, age and phase of season moderated the effects in the results section, and there was significant small-study bias at every distance.
paper.limitations: The reviewed studies were mostly parallel-group trials in male soccer players, and some subgroups had very few training groups. Effects are within-group pre-to-post changes, heterogeneity was high, and there was evidence of publication bias. Secondary and combined-specific results changed significance when single studies were removed. The abstract and discussion say playing standard moderated the effect (sub-elite greater than elite at 0-5 m), but the results section reports no significant difference by playing standard.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and performance staff of football code athletes may use combined or tertiary (strength, power, plyometric) work to develop short-sprint speed, as these had the largest evidence base. Resisted or assisted sprinting also improved times, but on few studies whose significance was sensitive to single-study removal, and sprint-only or sport-only training did not show a significant average gain.
paper.athleteDev: For football code athletes, short-sprint development can draw on combined programmes, resisted or assisted sprinting, and strength, power or plyometric training, since the authors found no single method clearly superior. The gains are average pre-to-post changes in athletes with limited prior exposure to these methods, and individual responses varied.
paper.rtp: The review includes only healthy, non-injured athletes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport sprint training or clearance. It says nothing about the safety or effectiveness of these methods after injury.

records.sourceFile: The use of acute exercise interventions as game day priming strategies to improve physical performance and athlete readiness in team-sport athletes - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Mason B, McKune A, Pumpa K, Ball N. The Use of Acute Exercise Interventions as Game Day Priming Strategies to Improve Physical Performance and Athlete Readiness in Team-Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of acute exercise interventions, applied 1 to 12 h before competition, as priming strategies for team-sport athletes. Twenty-nine studies were included. Heavy, low-volume resistance training improved strength and power after 4 to 6 h, running sprints improved subsequent sprint performance after 5 to 6 h, and evidence for endurance running or cycling was limited.
paper.tldr: Heavy, low-volume resistance training done 4 to 6 hours before testing improved strength and power in the included studies, and maximal sprint running improved later sprint performance in two rugby studies. Endurance work showed little benefit as priming, and the evidence base is small.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of SPORTDiscus, PubMed and CENTRAL, with the last search on 26 February 2020. Eligible studies were randomised or non-randomised comparative studies in healthy adults aged 18 to 40 with pre-post outcomes and an exercise intervention 1 to 12 h before testing. Studies using nutrition, supplements, heat or cold priming, stretching, massage, vibration or altitude were excluded. Two reviewers screened; PEDro scores were assigned, and studies were grouped into resistance training, cycling, running and other interventions.
paper.findings: Twenty-nine studies were included. Resistance training with heavy loads at low volume increased strength and power after a 4 to 6 h recovery, with limited improvement after 1 to 3 h or 6 to 12 h. Running-based sprint priming improved subsequent sprint and repeat-sprint performance after 5 to 6 h. Cycling improved counter-movement jump height in one study only. No significant differences were reported after endurance running or cycling. Hormone and blood lactate responses were mixed, and in one study (Saez de Villareal et al.) loaded countermovement jump height improved only after a loaded countermovement jump protocol.
paper.limitations: Methodological approaches differed too much for direct comparison, with some studies comparing against pre-trial values, others against control trials or other interventions, and sample sizes were small relative to the large inter- and intra-individual variation in hormone responses. Few studies were designed to test a priming intervention, most measured responses to different exercise bouts across a 1 to 12 h period in varied populations, and PEDro scores were only 4 to 6 out of 10.
paper.practicalImplications: Team-sport practitioners who want heavy strength or power work to carry over to a match may consider low-volume heavy resistance training 4 to 6 h before competition, provided total volume is kept low. The review does not support endurance running or cycling as a priming strategy.
paper.athleteDev: Low-volume, heavy resistance work and maximal sprints done several hours before a session may improve strength, power and sprint performance in team-sport athletes. The effect windows and loads are drawn from small studies and should be tested in each squad.
paper.rtp: The review includes only healthy adults with no pain, injury or illness, so it cannot inform return-to-sport priming or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: The worst-case scenario - Recovery between repeated high intensity efforts in rugby league match play.pdf

paper.citation: Gabbett TJ. The "Worst-Case Scenario": Recovery Between Repeated High-Intensity Efforts in Rugby League Match-Play. Sports Health. 2022.
paper.abstract: Among 104 semi-elite rugby league players from 11 teams tracked by GPS over 28 matches, most repeated high-intensity efforts were followed by 10 seconds or less of recovery. Top 4 teams performed a somewhat greater proportion of these very-short-recovery efforts than Bottom 4 teams.
paper.tldr: In semi-elite rugby league, most repeated high-intensity efforts in matches came after 10 seconds or less of recovery. Top 4 teams had a slightly higher share of these very-short-recovery efforts than Bottom 4 teams.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort observational study of 104 male semi-elite players from 11 Queensland Cup teams. Movement and collisions were recorded with 10 Hz GPS units with accelerometer and gyroscope in 28 matches. An RHIE bout was defined as three or more high-acceleration, high-speed or contact efforts across recovery periods of up to 120 seconds, and recovery between efforts was binned into five durations. Teams were split into Top 4 and Bottom 4 by ladder position, and effect sizes with confidence limits were used for comparisons.
paper.findings: Most RHIE recoveries were 10 seconds or less in both groups. Top 4 teams had 58.2% of bouts with 10 seconds or less recovery versus 49.8% for Bottom 4 teams (effect size 0.27 +/- 0.19, 98% very likely). Differences in the 61 to 120 second band were trivial (effect size 0.17). Top 4 wide-running forwards had a higher share of 10-second-or-less bouts than Bottom 4 wide-running forwards (62.2% vs 44.6%, effect size 0.59), and Top 4 teams had a small first-half excess of these bouts (60.8% vs 52.7% in the second half).
paper.limitations: Single competition (Queensland Cup, semi-elite) with 28 matches, and GPS device numbers limited which matches could be covered. Team differences in tactics and in attacking or defensive phases were not quantified, and video was not aligned with GPS data, so the positional differences cannot be explained. The RHIE definition differs from the 21-second definition used in earlier studies. The players in this study are semi-elite and the findings may not transfer to full-time professional squads.
paper.practicalImplications: In this sample, most match RHIE bouts involved 10 seconds or less between efforts, so conditioning for semi-elite rugby league can include repeated high-speed, collision and tackle efforts with very short recovery. Lower-ranked teams could include training that targets rapid recovery between efforts, particularly for wide-running forwards. The study does not show that such training improves match results.
paper.athleteDev: Semi-elite players in this study performed most RHIE bouts with 10 seconds or less recovery, so training can include efforts with very short recovery to match match demands. The data are descriptive, so they support the match-demand profile rather than proving that this training improves outcomes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes match demands in uninjured players and does not measure injury, rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Throwing cold water on muscle growth - A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy.pdf

paper.citation: Piñero A, Burke R, Augustin F, Mohan AE, DeJesus K, Sapuppo M, et al. Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy. European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-13.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of eight randomized trials comparing resistance training with cold water immersion after each session against resistance training alone. The pooled comparison favored resistance training alone for muscle growth, but the credible interval included zero, and study quality was mostly fair to poor.
paper.tldr: Cold water immersion straight after resistance training may slightly reduce muscle growth compared with training alone. The authors urge caution because the trials are small and of fair to poor quality, and the finding applies only to immersion within about 15 minutes of training.
paper.methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 24 February 2023, with reference-list checks. The review was preregistered and followed PRISMA. Eight randomized trials were pooled with Bayesian random-effects models. Study quality was rated with two tools: SMART-LD, developed for resistance training research, and the Downs and Black checklist.
paper.findings: Uncontrolled effects showed resistance training alone produced muscle growth (SMD 0.36, 95% CrI 0.10 to 0.61), while cold water immersion plus resistance training produced small-to-negligible growth (SMD 0.14, 95% CrI -0.08 to 0.36). The comparative effect favored resistance training alone (cSMD -0.22, 95% CrI -0.47 to 0.04). Meta-regression found no clear moderation by training status, study duration or training frequency.
paper.limitations: Muscle growth was measured with different methods (DXA, biopsy, ultrasound, MRI and circumference), and training programs varied, with few multi-joint or whole-body protocols. Nutrition was rarely tracked, and cold water timing and temperature varied little across studies. The findings apply to immersion within 15 minutes after exercise, not to cryotherapy or intermittent use.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes whose goal is maximal muscle size may avoid cold water immersion immediately after resistance sessions, and may consider the timing and frequency of any cooling. The authors note that cryotherapy and intermittent cooling were not tested for long-term muscle growth.
paper.athleteDev: The trials used young adults, not youth athletes, and included no adolescents. The review therefore cannot show whether post-session cold water immersion affects muscle growth in developing athletes.
paper.rtp: The review excluded trials of people with musculoskeletal injury and included no return-to-sport outcomes. It cannot show whether cold water immersion helps or delays rehabilitation or the return to training.

records.sourceFile: Time course of neuromuscular, hormonal, and perceptual responses following moderate and high-load resistance priming exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Harrison PW, James LP, Jenkins DG, McGuigan MR, Schuster RW, Kelly VG. Time Course of Neuromuscular, Hormonal, and Perceptual Responses Following Moderate- and High-Load Resistance Priming Exercise. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Fifteen males with at least 12 months of strength training completed control, high-load (87% 1RM) and moderate-load (65% 1RM) half-squat sessions in a randomised, counterbalanced crossover design. Countermovement jump, squat jump, salivary hormones and perceptual measures were taken before and up to 32 hours after each session.
paper.tldr: A heavy half-squat primer gave a small squat-jump gain about 8 hours later, and a moderate-load primer gave small jump gains the next afternoon. Control sessions improved by a similar amount at 32 hours, so the priming effect is not isolated.
paper.methods: Randomised, counterbalanced crossover with control, high-load and moderate-load sessions, each separated by 3 to 6 days. Force-plate jumps, salivary testosterone and cortisol, and a 100 mm visual analogue perceptual questionnaire were measured before and at 5 minutes, 8, 24 and 32 hours after each session. Results are percentage change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals and Cliff delta.
paper.findings: After high-load priming, squat jump height rose 4.5% at 8 hours (95% CI 2.2 to 6.8; Cliff delta 0.20), and countermovement jump height fell 3.7% at 5 minutes; at 24 hours squat jump height was unchanged while jump time rose, perceived fatigue rose and perceived performance fell. After moderate-load priming, countermovement jump rose 6.1% (95% CI 2.1 to 7.8) and squat jump 6.5% (95% CI 1.2 to 11.8) at 32 hours, while control sessions rose 3.9% and 4.5%. Salivary testosterone fell at 8 and 32 hours after both priming loads and cortisol fell in the afternoons, but the authors judged that priming did not considerably influence hormone status.
paper.limitations: No direct between-condition comparison was possible because of repeated testing, and the authors note that control gains may reflect repeated jump testing. The sample was 15 strength-trained males rather than elite athletes, and the changes are small relative to measurement error. The abstract's 'similar improvements' after moderate load is not separated from the control response.
paper.practicalImplications: A morning heavy half-squat primer may give a small squat-jump gain later that day, and a moderate-load primer may help the following afternoon. The authors caution that priming the day before an early-morning session does not appear optimal and may be detrimental after heavy loads. Because control sessions produced similar late gains, treat these as possible rather than confirmed priming effects.
paper.athleteDev: Shows that a single session of heavy or moderate half squats can slightly change jump output for hours to a day later, which may help plan a pre-training or pre-competition primer. It does not show a performance gain that exceeds the control response.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the sample was uninjured strength-trained males and no return-to-sport outcome was measured.

records.sourceFile: To Couple or not to Couple For Acute-Chronic Workload Ratios and Injury Risk, Does it Really Matter.pdf

paper.citation: Gabbett TJ, Hulin B, Blanch P, Chapman P, Bailey D. To Couple or not to Couple? For Acute:Chronic Workload Ratios and Injury Risk, Does it Really Matter? Int J Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: The authors compared coupled and uncoupled acute:chronic workload ratios (ACWR) and injury risk in 28 elite cricket fast bowlers, with workload estimated from session-RPE. The two methods were almost perfectly related (R2 = 0.99). No significant differences in injury risk were found between them, and higher ACWRs were linked to greater injury likelihood under both methods.
paper.tldr: Coupled and uncoupled workload ratios gave the same injury-risk pattern in this cricket group, so the choice between them matters less than has been argued. Staff can keep their current method and convert between the two if needed.
paper.methods: Re-analysis of previously collected session-RPE and injury data from 28 elite cricket fast bowlers. Coupled ratios used a 1-week acute and 4-week chronic workload that includes the acute week; uncoupled ratios used the latest week against the prior 3 weeks. Injury risk by ratio category was compared using percentile-rank and discrete-category methods, with binary logistic regression and relative risks.
paper.findings: The two ACWR methods were almost perfectly related by a second-order polynomial (R2 = 0.99). Converting coupled ratios to uncoupled values shifted the injury-likelihood curve to the right above a ratio of 1.0. Using the original data, injury likelihood rose with higher ratios under both methods, with no significant difference between coupled and uncoupled ratios in any percentile or discrete category.
paper.limitations: One cohort of 28 cricket fast bowlers from one sport, with injuries defined as non-contact events that caused lost match time or more than one missed training session in a week. The authors note the analysis shows association, not that injury can be predicted from one training variable, and that the uncoupled method is statistically cleaner even though the practical difference is small.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners can keep their current coupled or uncoupled ACWR method, stay consistent, and convert between them with the paper's equation if needed. When applying coupled thresholds such as 1.5 or 2.0 to uncoupled ratios, the authors suggest converting the categories, though they note unconverted thresholds reproduced the same rising-risk pattern; ACWR should be read alongside wellness and readiness measures.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Workload monitoring teams can keep their existing ratio method and use the conversion to compare results across methods. Use the ratio as one input alongside wellness and readiness data when planning training loads, and build sport-specific injury models where the data allow.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Cannot inform return to sport. The study looks at non-contact injury risk from training and match loads and does not assess injured players or rehabilitation loading.

records.sourceFile: Train the Engine or the Brakes - Influence of Momentum on the Change of Direction Deficit.pdf

paper.citation: Fernandes R, Bishop C, Turner AN, Chavda S, Maloney SJ. Train the Engine or the Brakes? Influence of Momentum on the Change of Direction Deficit. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Seventeen academy soccer players completed jump, sprint and 505 tests to see whether momentum, speed and jump measures explain change of direction deficit (COD-D). No regression predictor of COD-D was found, but when players were split by COD-D, those with the smaller deficit were faster on the 505 test and tended to be slower over 10 m and carry less momentum, though these differences were not significant.
paper.tldr: In academy soccer players, speed and jump measures did not explain change of direction deficit. Faster players carrying more momentum may show larger deficits, but this is a non-significant subgroup pattern, not a tested intervention effect.
paper.methods: Seventeen male academy soccer players performed single-leg countermovement and drop jumps, a 40-m sprint with 0-10 m and 30-40 m splits, and the 505 test on both legs over two sessions. Momentum was calculated as the split velocity multiplied by body mass. Multiple regression, Pearson correlations, and a median split by COD-D (n = 8 per group) with Cohen effect sizes were used.
paper.findings: Regression did not identify significant predictors of COD-D on either leg. COD-D correlated with 505 time (r = .65 to .69) but not with acceleration, maximum velocity, momentum or jump measures. In the median split, the smaller-COD-D group was faster on the 505 test (effect size -1.24, P = .03) and tended to be slower over 0-10 m (d = 0.79, P = .33) and to carry less momentum (d = -0.81, P = .17).
paper.limitations: The sample was 17 male academy players, with no strength measures and no control for maturation, which the authors note could not be discounted. The median-split comparisons are underpowered and the momentum and acceleration differences were not significant. The abstract gives P < .001 for the 505 comparison, but Table 3 gives P = .03 for CODS and P < .001 for COD-D; the table values were used.
paper.practicalImplications: COD-D and 505 time may rank athletes similarly but should not be used interchangeably. For fast players with high momentum and a larger deficit, the authors suggest eccentric-biased or technique-focused change of direction training, while noting that its effectiveness has not been tested.
paper.athleteDev: Use COD-D alongside 505 time to build a fuller profile of each academy player. Fast players who carry high momentum may need eccentric-biased or technical change of direction work, but this is a hypothesis from one small cross-sectional study.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested injury-free academy players and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Training alters joint power distributions during running in National Football League Draft Preparation Players.pdf

paper.citation: Mokha GM, Bonsangue M, Brezina T, Haberer J. Training alters joint power distributions during running in National Football League Draft Preparation Players. Sports Biomechanics. 2025.
paper.abstract: Fifty-two American football players ran on a treadmill at 5.5 to 6.5 m/s before and after a six-week NFL draft preparation camp. Negative (absorbed) total limb power fell on the left limb, mainly because negative ankle power decreased bilaterally, and the left hip's share of negative power rose. Total positive power and most joint-level positive power did not change significantly.
paper.tldr: Over a six-week draft camp, these players absorbed less power at the ankle while running at the same speed, which may point to a change in running mechanics. With no control group, the camp cannot be confirmed as the cause.
paper.methods: Single 5-second treadmill runs were recorded before and after the camp at a matched mean speed of 6.4 m/s, using 10-camera motion capture (120 Hz) and an instrumented split-belt treadmill (1000 Hz). Joint power was calculated by inverse dynamics and normalised to body mass, and each joint's share of total positive and negative power was compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests because the knee data were non-normal.
paper.findings: Negative total limb power decreased on both limbs, significantly on the left (Z = -2.113, P = .035, r = .30). Negative ankle power decreased on the left (P = .049, r = .27) and right (P = .009, r = .36). The left hip's share of negative power increased (P = .016, r = .31). Total positive power did not change, and the shifts in positive joint shares were not significant.
paper.limitations: The study had no control group and a convenience sample of 52 players, with 23 of 75 recruited players excluded for speed, marker or running-pattern reasons. Shoes were not controlled, and the authors note that position groups were not analysed. Figure and text cross-references are inconsistent, and Table 2 contains a CI typo for the right ankle.
paper.practicalImplications: Drill-based speed mechanics work during a camp may change how players share joint power while running, but the change was not consistent across players. Coaches who track joint-level running mechanics before and after a block may be able to see whether technique work changes power sharing.
paper.athleteDev: Use this study as a hypothesis for speed-mechanics work in football players: drill-based camp work may reduce reliance on ankle absorption in some players, and joint power shares could be tracked across a block. The effects were small to medium and varied between players, so they need checking in each group.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested players who had been cleared for a training camp and measured no injuries or return-to-play outcomes, so the authors' comments about possible injury protection were not tested.

records.sourceFile: Training for muscular strength - Methods for monitoring and adjusting training intensity.pdf

paper.citation: Suchomel TJ, Nimphius S, Bellon CR, Hornsby WG, Stone MH. Training for Muscular Strength: Methods for Monitoring and Adjusting Training Intensity. Sports Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: This review compares methods for adjusting resistance training intensity, including linear loading, the two-for-two rule, percent of one repetition maximum, repetition maximum zones, rating of perceived exertion and repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, autoregulatory progressive resistance exercise and velocity-based training. The authors conclude that methods which account for daily readiness, such as RPE, repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, APRE and velocity-based training, can be combined with outcome and process measures to guide practitioners.
paper.tldr: No single intensity method suits every athlete. Linear loading and fixed percentages of 1RM miss daily readiness, while RPE, set-repetition best, APRE and velocity-based training adjust to it. Combining these with longer-term monitoring is the authors' recommendation.
paper.methods: Narrative review of resistance training intensity methods, covering the advantages, limitations and practical use of each method. The review also discusses how motor learning and process measures could be added to outcome-based monitoring. No search strategy is described.
paper.findings: The authors report that linear loading can produce a plateau or overreaching if used for long periods, and that %1RM and RM zones fail to account for daily fluctuations in performance. They describe RPE, repetitions in reserve, set-repetition best, APRE and velocity-based training as more responsive to daily readiness, and cite comparison studies in which APRE and set-repetition best produced strength gains similar to or greater than linear loading or RM zones in some trials.
paper.limitations: No systematic search or quality appraisal is described, so the selection of studies is not transparent. The cited comparisons vary in design, sample and method of RPE or velocity measurement, and the authors note that RPE and repetitions in reserve accuracy and velocity-based 1RM prediction are not yet established across populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Use outcome measures (such as load and velocity) alongside subjective readiness measures, rather than a single fixed-percentage prescription, and be cautious with novices, since RPE accuracy depends on experience. Keep track of longer-term training volume and intensity so that stagnation or overreaching can be spotted.
paper.athleteDev: Strength coaches can combine RPE or repetitions in reserve with velocity-based or set-repetition best methods to adjust loads from day to day, while watching for technique loss near failure. The review gives a framework for choosing methods, not a tested ranking of their effects on strength.
paper.rtp: The review mentions rehabilitation and return from injury only in passing, and it does not evaluate return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to judge when an athlete's strength is ready for sport.

records.sourceFile: Training interventions for improved deceleration ability in adult team-based field sports athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature.pdf

paper.citation: Marvin LA, Read P, McLean B, Palmer S, Fransen J. Training Interventions for Improved Deceleration Ability in Adult Team-Based Field Sports Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Literature. Int J Strength Cond. 2024.
paper.abstract: Twelve randomised controlled trials in adult team field and court athletes were reviewed, and nine were pooled across 29 deceleration-specific outcomes. Training interventions did not improve deceleration performance compared with control groups (SMD -0.04, 95% CI -0.50 to 0.42), and the risk of bias was high in all studies.
paper.tldr: Current randomised trials do not show that general training improves deceleration performance in team athletes more than usual training does. Because these trials used mostly non-specific interventions and had high risk of bias, the result is inconclusive rather than a verdict against deceleration training.
paper.methods: Systematic search of SPORTDiscus, PubMed and Web of Science, followed by PRISMA-guided screening (registered on OSF) for randomised controlled trials with a control group and pre-post deceleration outcomes in adult team-field and court athletes. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, and post-intervention Hedges g values were pooled using a multilevel random-effects model with Knapp-Hartung confidence intervals.
paper.findings: Across all deceleration performance outcomes, the pooled SMD was -0.04 (95% CI -0.50 to 0.42), with negative values favouring control groups and I2 = 0%. Secondary kinetic outcomes favoured control groups (SMD -0.29, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.25; joint kinetics -0.20, 95% CI -1.01 to 0.61), joint kinematics slightly favoured interventions (SMD 0.07, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.24), and muscle activation favoured control groups (SMD -0.10, 95% CI -0.44 to 0.24). All of these confidence intervals cross zero, so none of the pooled effects was statistically significant.
paper.limitations: Only 12 small RCTs were found, nine were pooled, and most outcomes were measured in one or two studies. All studies had high overall risk of bias, and the pooled outcomes came from different protocols and definitions. The text reports 380 participants, while the abstract reports 381.
paper.practicalImplications: The evidence does not yet show that general strength, plyometric, eccentric or agility work improves deceleration more than usual training. The authors suggest that deceleration-specific, sport-representative training may transfer better, but no included trial tested this, so it remains a hypothesis.
paper.athleteDev: Do not assume that adding general strength, plyometric or agility blocks will improve how athletes decelerate. If deceleration is a priority, deceleration-specific work tracked with the same test each time is a reasonable choice, but current trials do not identify a method that reliably works.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return to sport. It included trained athletes in intervention trials and did not study injured players or return-to-play criteria.
